newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Grain-Wheat plant starts with good rain.
newsitem.headline: Australian Grain-Wheat plant starts with good rain.

text.p: Winter wheat sowing in northern districts of Australia's eastern grainbelt has hit top gear as good rain eased fears about the new crop outlook.

The main rain has fallen in the state of New South Wales (NSW), the country's biggest wheat area in 1996/97, which last week received good soaking rain in its northwest and central areas and useful rain in its southern regions.
Victoria and the big producing state of Western Australia also received lighter and patchier rain.
"There's a lot of diesel being burnt now," said NSW-based Bill Mitchell of New England Agricultural Traders (NEAT). "A lot of people have started (to plant)."
Some areas were still looking for planting rains, but rainfall had generally been good, he said.
Guy Allen of GrainCorp also said heavy planting activity over the NSW grain belt, after the rain, was expected to continue in the coming week for wheat and canola.
Bureau of Meteorology officials in main centres confirmed to Reuters on Friday that good rain had been received in extensive area of NSW.
Victoria and Western Australia still needed rain despite some useful falls, they said.
But Australia's long dry autumn, the driest on record in some areas, has left its sceptics about the coming crop.
Rain in NSW had improved initial crop prospects but good follow-on rain was still needed in Australia's southeast, broker Gary Booth of Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming Futures said.
The El Nino weather pattern also remained, making the prospect of good follow-on rain less likely, he said.

Australia would have a large area sown again this year if only because many farmers had bought new machinery in the past two years. "(Still) there is quite a degree of doubt about the follow-up rainfall," he said.
NEAT's Mitchell now sees Australia headed for an 18.0-20.0 million tonne wheat crop after latest rain, up from the pre-rain view of a likely 17.00-20.0 million tonne crop.
The Australian Wheat Board's (AWB) early estimate put Australia's 1997/98 wheat crop at 18.0-19.0 million tonnes.
Independent forecaster Australian Wheat Forecasters Pty Ltd early this month put the expected wheat crop at 17.89 million tonnes, down from last year's record 23.6 million tonnes.
Allen described markets as fairly quiet during the latest week with increased activity on Thursday and Friday on the rain.
Wheat cash prices fell over the past week, reflecting better crop prospects.

A A$5.00 a tonne price fall for sorghum was the grains market's main feature. Sorghum fell to about A$162.00 a tonne delivered Sydney, in trading so thin that it was hard to establish a price with much confidence, Mitchell said.

The main pressure on sorghum was a falling international market, down by about US$10.00 a tonne fob, on large sales by Argentina to Japan. Australian end users had their requirements covered for May and June and possibly into July, he said.
Allen saw the sorghum price down by A$5.00-A$6.00 a tonne to about A$164.00 Newcastle, on lack of demand by end users.
Old crop cash wheat prices fell by A$6.00-A$7.00 a tonne to about A$194.00-A$196.00, while new crop wheat ended at about A$168.00 on Friday, down from A$174.00 earlier in the week, Allen said.
Mitchell saw old crop wheat as generally holding its cash price in the past week because of the continuing supply squeeze.
New crop wheat fell A$4.00-A$5.00 to A$170.00 on Chicago's fall, and appeared likely to continue to edge back in line with the U.S., he said.
Some end user demand for barley also emerged during the week although prices generally remained unchanged.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
